title: Why Gil lets his soloists stretch out
summary: Gil says that with little work he lets players solo as long as they want, though pieces have a natural length.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: No, lately I haven't been working very much so whenever I get a chance to work I don't really care about the audience because I'm so hungry to play that I just as soon let the players all play on every number all that they want to because it gives me more chances to be active musically you see.

That's what I've been doing and of course, some people like it and some people think it's just terrible. So, naturally you couldn't go on like that for ever because each piece has its own natural length really and its own, the emotional part, the emotional content is lively, meaningful then it can go on until it's not you know. Until you've said what you're going to say. and then it's up to somebody to... I haven't gotten to that with this band yet because we really haven't worked that much............
Now I'm down at the Village Gate I'll be cutting down somewhat on the improvised time.
Well this is what I was going...
Sometimes it works out fine and
So the extended solos are not necessarily of the same length?
No. Sometimes they are. There are a couple of tunes where they are marked a definite number of choruses even though it's a long time. But most of the time they are not.
